en: The sixty women singing laments,
With Akylai at their head,
All scattered and fled.
Kyrgylchal, chief of the forty,
And Tazbaimat together,
As they made ready to mount their horses,
As they fled in among the six scoundrels,
Your leopard sister-in-law Kanykey
Caught Kyrgylchal, chief of the forty,
By the lower hem.
Falling short of reaching his kidney,
His rump as broad as a millstone—
She sliced away half of it.
He lost his wits in confusion
And was thrown into panic;
From the near side, Tazbaimat
Had fled.
“If God truly supports me,
If Bahauddin truly comes to my aid,
If my gray-maned hero gone to the other world
Truly has a spirit,”
Kanykey raged,
Saying this in anger.
Your precious sister-in-law Kanykey
Turned toward the True One.
The familiar Tazbaimat,
As he was fleeing,
She struck him with Ak-Tinte.
The lower part of his right shoulder-blade
Ak-Tinte gouged through;
Two of his ribs
Ak-Tinte cut through.
Tazbaimat and Kyrgylchal
Were in a whirl of dust,
Dappled red with blood.
Surkyzyl and Kertelki
Paced with every stride;
From those wounded, accursed men,
Blood flowing from their bodies
Streamed over their saddlecloths.
“Alas, alas, my back!” they cried.
“As a wife, she divided customs and disrupted the people;
Your shameless shrew has devoured us,” they said.
“As a girl, she shook the world and disrupted the people;
She has brought us to ruin,” they said.
“She has dug a deep pit,” they said.
“She has boiled up misery,” they said.
“She has a secure backing;
Your wild sister-in-law, that shrew,
Has somewhere she relies upon.
Six thousand silver ingots and a thousand beaver pelts
Bakai has taken as a bribe;
To Ormombek of Tekeche
He seems ready to smuggle her away.
His tale is worth the world.
It seems she would not marry you even if you killed her.
If Kanykey takes it into her head,
She could plunder your fine cloth,
Could wreak havoc this very year.
If anyone goes as a mediator,
She will seize him like this
And rip him apart on the road;
If Kanykey gets her way,
She could set the dogs upon us.”
To their khans Abyke and Kobosh,
Kyrgylchal and Tazbaimat came and told it,
To all six scoundrels.
To scatter her four kinds of livestock—
God had truly struck the scoundrels now—
The prince's wife Kanykey,
They meant to trample her down,
To plunder her fine cloth,
To wreak thorough havoc.
If she obeyed, one of the six would take her;
If your sister-in-law would not obey,
They would bring calamity upon her head.
Semetey, still being lulled in arms—
They made a firm compact:
He was still an infant in the cradle;
They would drag him along the road
And have the dogs tear him apart.
By force, Kanykey
Would be taken by one of the six.
They would give her a torn black yurt,
Give her a maimed black cow,
To the nearby cattle herdsman—
They would make her his milkmaid.
They made a firm compact
To take their far-reaching vengeance on the shrew,
Make her ride a bay mare,
Dress her in a felt cloak,
Of the departed falcon Manas
Make her feel his death in this way,
Cut her soles and rub in salt.
If she consented, one of the six would take her;
If your sister-in-law would not consent,
They would simply kill her.
Chewing white wheat flour,
The six scoundrels stood in a row,
Holding the sacred Quran,
Making their compact firm,
Swearing an oath upon their lives.
Within that oath were
Abyke and Kobosh, two scoundrels;
Chyibyt and Kochkor made four;
Adybai and Kolbai made six.
With a pale mottled pennant for their banner,
When the two went forth as khans:
“If she acts like this, the bitch will let nothing go right;
She will never leave us unharmed.
If her orphan son grows up,
He will not let us turn the plow;
He will not let us remain in this Talas.
He will not let us ride a mare with a mane,
Will not let us eat a lamb with a fat tail,
Will not let us fit the yoke-pins,
Will not let us plow in spring,
Will not let us open the earth,
Will not let us scatter a handful of seed.
There is malice in her eyes;
If that bitch has the power,
She means to strike me down.
Crookedness shows in her eyes;
Deceit runs through her words.
If that bitch finds her chance,
She means to do away with me.
As though her slayer of foes were still alive,
She will not listen to my words.
Making an example of my mediator,
My bitch has made a fool of me.
If the shrew is willing to marry,
Let us get her answer today.
If the shrew will not marry,
Let us bring calamity upon her head today!
Let us see how brave she is.
The countless riches left by Manas, slayer of foes—
Let us divide them today by the measure of the whip.
Let us trample her down,
Scatter her four kinds of livestock today,
Raid and take her mares,
Let us exact our far-reaching revenge.
If the bitch comes near,
Let us beat her brains out,
Cut down her willows and fell them,
Tear down all her buildings,
Make her a sheath fitted to a sword,
Make the damned woman a spectacle before the sun.
If she will not marry, upon her head
Let us bring trouble no mortal has known,
So that henceforth widows
Will conduct themselves as widows,
Making her an example to the people.”
So saying, the six scoundrels
Made ready their battle-axes,
As though Alooke's Kongurbai,
As though the Chinese had come from far away
And were besieging their village.
They readied spears and guns,
Beat their drums,
Gathered all the troops they had,
Set their unerring marksmen
To close in along the edges,
And chose skilled spearmen;
They had gathered
The best men who could devise a plan.
A mighty one among the forty companions,
Yrchyuul, son of Yraman Khan,
Displeased with the men,
Refusing to obey the wicked,
Amid the forty companions
Spoke these words:
“When gray-maned Manas was alive,
Whenever we wished, we ourselves
Would descend along Kok-Zhaiyk.
The dark-complexioned beauty,
The radiant one among Muslim women,
My dear sister-in-law Kanykey—
We would taste food from her hand.
Yesterday, in the hollow of Zhylgynduu,
Along the broad Talas,
When the Argyn and Kyrgyz had come down to the hollow
And were camped there,
With fermented mare's milk by day and women by night,
When that was how we lived,
Our marten-fur caps, made in pairs,
Swaying as we went,
Joining and governing the world,
When we lived in joy,
One of us came without a horse;
Will his spirit not strike us?
For the companion who came without a horse,
Wild-sheep feet and copper forelegs—
He provided a noble steed to ride!
One of us came without a coat;
For the companion who came without a coat,
A golden collar and copper sleeves,
Double mail with rings like larks' eyes,
A striped-cloth robe, a roomy jacket—
He clothed him in the finest coat!
For the companion who came without a people,
He allotted Argyns and gave him rule over them!
For the companion who came without a wife,
Crimson dresses and moon-slender waists,
Thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
Roving eyes that stirred desire—
When did he ever begrudge his girls?!
One of us companions came without livestock;
For the companion who came without livestock,
Mottled-headed horses on the foothills,
Thoroughbreds and swift steeds together,
Great Manas allotted them.
He joined what was broken of yours,
Gathered what was scattered of yours,
Kindled your extinguished fire,
Revived your dead soul,
Made you a khan endowed with sacred power,
Made you a man equal to himself.
We became heroes come to full maturity;
Since coming to Khan Manas,
We became the equals of heroes' sons.
We became a firmly built walled house;
Since coming to Khan Manas,
We became illustrious khans!
The generous one who treated us like this—
How can we attack his wife?
Our dear friend gone to the other world—
How can we piss upon his salt?!
Our gray-maned hero gone to the other world—
How can we plunder his palace?
Semetey, whom he had thus begotten,
Was still an infant in the cradle;
How can we beat the hero's child?
He who gave his hand to twelve saints,
The precious one gone to the other world—
How can we plunder his palace?!
Since we came to Talas,
Her eyes shining like a wild sheep's,
My precious sister-in-law Kanykey
Cared for us in a mother's place.
Since we came to this Kanykey,
She gave us honey stirred into spirits,
Gave us meat served in gold,
Clothed us in coats no bullet could pierce,
To Beijing, beyond the reach of the Four Companions,
She enabled you to extend your strength.
You have forgotten, forty companions,
Your prince who has gone to the other world.
How can we now plunder
Your mother in Talas, a woman like Kanykey?
If the oath strikes, will it not strike us?
Will his spirit not destroy us?!
Damn your fathers' graves, forty companions!
All forty of you were dogs from forty different places;
Your friend gone to the other world—
We have turned away from him like this,
If not dogs, what sort of people were we!
